nameStory: The Northern Tessellated Darter gets its name from its beautiful mosaic-like pattern that resembles tessellated tiles or a stained glass window. 'Tessellated' comes from the Latin word 'tessella,' meaning small square stones used in ancient mosaics, perfectly describing the checkerboard pattern that decorates this little fish's sides.
description: The Northern Tessellated Darter is a small, slender fish that rarely grows longer than 3-4 inches, making it one of New England's more petite freshwater species. Its body is covered in a striking checkerboard pattern of dark squares and lighter spaces, giving it an almost artistic appearance. Like other darters, it has a torpedo-shaped body built for quick bursts of movement along stream bottoms, and it lacks the swim bladder that most fish use for buoyancy. This bottom-dweller prefers to 'dart' from rock to rock rather than swim continuously through the water column.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Distinctive checkerboard or tessellated pattern of dark squares on lighter background along the sides, creating a mosaic-like appearance that's unmistakable once you see it

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender, torpedo-shaped body that feels firm and muscular when handled, built for quick darting movements rather than sustained swimming

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two separate dorsal fins on the back, with the first having sharp spines that feel prickly to the touch and the second being soft-rayed

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish typically 2-4 inches long, easily fitting in the palm of your hand with room to spare

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found on rocky or gravelly stream bottoms where it rests motionless between quick darting movements, often hiding among stones

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth positioned at the front tip of the head, perfectly sized for picking small insects and larvae from crevices between rocks

habitat: Northern Tessellated Darters live in clear, cool streams and rivers throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with rocky or gravelly bottoms where they can dart between stones. They prefer moderate to swift-flowing water with good oxygen levels, often found in riffles and shallow runs where insects are abundant. You'll typically spot them in streams that also support trout, as they prefer similar clean, well-oxygenated water conditions.

seasonality.spring: Spawning season brings increased activity as males develop brighter colors and can be seen defending small territories among the rocks. Look for them in shallow, gravelly areas where females deposit eggs.
seasonality.summer: Most active during daylight hours in cooler morning and evening periods, often hiding under rocks during the heat of the day. This is the best time for observation as the water is clear and low.
seasonality.fall: Feeding heavily before winter, making them more visible as they actively hunt for insects and small invertebrates throughout the day.
seasonality.winter: Less active in cold water, often hiding deep in rock crevices and moving very little, making them difficult to spot during this season.

funFact: Northern Tessellated Darters don't have swim bladders like most fish, which means they literally sink like stones if they stop swimming - but they've turned this apparent disadvantage into a superpower, allowing them to rest on the bottom without fighting buoyancy and dart with lightning speed to catch prey or escape predators.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the closely related Johnny Darter, but the Northern Tessellated Darter's checkerboard pattern is much more distinct and geometric. Remember: 'Tessellated equals tiles' - if you see a clear mosaic pattern, you've found the tessellated species.
contextualKnowledge: This species was formerly considered just a subspecies of the Johnny Darter until scientists recognized it as distinct. The name can be confusing since there are both 'Northern' and regular Tessellated Darters, but in New England waters, you're seeing the Northern variety.
compareHints: Compared to the Swamp Darter found in New England, the Northern Tessellated Darter has a much more pronounced checkerboard pattern and prefers flowing streams rather than still or slow-moving waters. The Fantail Darter, while similar in size, has a distinctively larger, fan-shaped tail fin and lacks the tessellated pattern. Both relatives have more muted, less geometric color patterns than the distinctive mosaic of the Northern Tessellated Darter.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relatives the northern tessellated darter and fantail darter, the swamp darter is the habitat specialist of the group — it's the only one that prefers slow, muddy waters over fast streams.
Unlike its relatives the Northern Tessellated Darter and Swamp Darter, the fantail darter has that unmistakable oversized, fan-shaped tail fin.
